clue.text: The poet sprang to it at Ghent

definitions.text: The poet sprang to it at Ghent

parts.words: The poet sprang to it at Ghent
parts.note: recalls the opening of Browning's poem about carrying good news from Ghent to Aix, where the rider leaps up onto his horse by the foot-rest

explanation.surface: A poet leaps into action in a Flemish city.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's 'How They Brought the Good News from Ghent to Aix' opens 'I sprang to the stirrup'; the clue quotes the line with the key word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The rider springs onto the saddle by its foot-loop, the metal hoop a horseman sets a boot in to mount.

clue.text: Hell in missile portrayed by count

indicators.note: the word for the underworld is placed inside the word for the missile

parts.note: SAM is a surface-to-air missile
Dis is the classical underworld, ruled by the god of that name

explanation.surface: A count depicts hell inside a rocket.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'count' is the Marquis (also styled Comte) de Sade, whose writings gave the vice its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The perversion of taking pleasure in cruelty is named after de Sade, who depicted it in his novels.

clue.text: Immediate as D. J. Enright's chronicles, and in …

definitions.meaning: the poet D. J. Enright published a verse sequence called ... Chronicles

explanation.surface: A poet's chronicles are as prompt as can be, and the thought runs on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing 'and in …' joins this clue to 3 Down, which completes the phrase 'in readiness', a near-synonym of 'immediate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Instant means occurring straight away; Enright's book title uses the word for brief, quickly caught poems.

clue.text: … this, as nereids may be

indicators.note: the sea-nymph letters could be rearranged into something else, so they are shuffled

parts.note: Nereids are the sea nymphs of Greek myth

explanation.surface: Sea nymphs are said to be in some state, continuing the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues 2 Down: 'Immediate ... and in … this' reads as 'and in readiness'; 'this' stands for the word that finishes that phrase. 'may be' rearranges AS NEREIDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a state of preparedness matches the idea of 'immediate' from the linked clue, ready at any moment.

clue.text: Mary Norton's hero's linen covers piano in dreadful complacency

parts.note: Pod is the father of the tiny family in Mary Norton's The Borrowers, with the possessive S

indicators.note: the word for household linen goes round the musical abbreviation for soft

parts.note: napery is table linen
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A children's-book hero's tablecloth is draped over a piano, smug and awful.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Podsnap in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend is the type of smug, insular self-satisfaction.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, from a Dickens character, names complacent philistine self-satisfaction that waves away anything unpleasant.

clue.text: Early woman judge, society girl, or a hopeful beginner?

parts.note: a deb is a debutante, a young woman entering society
taken as written

indicators.note: the beginning of the word hopeful supplies its first letter

explanation.surface: Asks whether an ancient female judge was a debutante or just an aspiring novice.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Book of Judges, Deborah was a prophetess who judged Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical prophetess was one of the judges of Israel, a woman leader in the earliest period of the nation.

clue.text: Misleading description of Eliot's rocks

parts.note: the rock in Eliot's The Waste Land is waterless, yet 'on the rocks' for a drink means served over ice, so a word for waterless misleads

explanation.surface: Someone describes a poet's rocks in a way that leads us astray.
explanation.walkthrough: The Waste Land's 'Here is no water but only rock' makes Eliot's rocks arid; a whisky on the rocks, though, is not served without ice or mixer.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterless, the condition of the barren rocks in Eliot's poem, and also the opposite of a drink served with ice.

clue.text: Eject convivial knight

definitions.meaning: to expel, as gas from the stomach
Sir Toby ... is the hard-drinking knight of Shakespeare's Twelfth Night

explanation.definitionFit: To burp is to expel wind noisily; Shakespeare's carousing Sir Toby bears the name.

clue.text: Sort of memory Austrian composer evidences of Hungarian born tunesmith

parts.note: ROM is read-only memory in computing
Alban Berg was an Austrian composer of the Second Viennese School

explanation.surface: A kind of memory and an Austrian composer bear witness to a Hungarian songwriter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sigmund Romberg, born in Hungary, wrote popular operettas such as The Student Prince.

clue.text: French novelist translating USA hymns

indicators.note: turning the American hymns into something else, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A French writer renders American hymns into another tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Joris-Karl Huysmans was the French author of the decadent novel A Rebours.

clue.text: It's wicked: a sad reflection on late French loony fringes

indicators.note: a mirror image reads the word sad from right to left

parts.note: tard is French for late

indicators.note: the fringes of loony are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A lament that something wicked happens, a sad comment on a dead, mad Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflection' turns SAD into DAS; 'late' looks like 'dead' but is the French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dastardly means mean and villainous, cowardly wickedness.

clue.text: English boat reminiscent of Coleridge's prison bower?

definitions.meaning: slang for a British ship or sailor
Coleridge's poem is 'This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison', so lime-like suggests that bower

explanation.surface: A British vessel recalls the leafy spot where Coleridge felt confined.
explanation.definitionFit: American slang for a British ship or sailor, also a fanciful adjective meaning like a lime tree.

clue.text: Narayan's sage took to the water with me

parts.note: to swim, past tense
I is the first person, as in me

explanation.surface: A holy man from an Indian novel went swimming with the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: R. K. Narayan's first novel is Swami and Friends.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hindu religious teacher; Narayan's schoolboy hero carries the title as his name.

clue.text: Pun mayhem, perhaps, in Lolita's sanctuary?

indicators.note: the pun mayhem could be arranged otherwise, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Wild wordplay might be found in Nabokov's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Lolita is Nabokov's 'nymphet', so her sanctuary is a shrine to the nymphs.
explanation.definitionFit: A grotto or shrine dedicated to nymphs, apt for the girl Nabokov calls a nymphet.

clue.text: Geneticist's boy heard happily-named composer

indicators.note: said out loud, the phrase becomes the composer's surname

parts.note: Gregor Mendel founded genetics; his son would be Mendel's son

explanation.surface: A gene scientist's son listens to a cheerfully named musician.
explanation.walkthrough: The composer's first name Felix means 'happy' in Latin, hence 'happily-named'.
explanation.definitionFit: Felix Mendelssohn, the German Romantic composer; Felix means fortunate or happy.

clue.text: Early chieftan in university, and the royal writer, become tedious

parts.note: taken as written
R stands for royal, as in Rex or Regina
a pen is a writing instrument
to drag on is to go on tiresomely long

explanation.surface: An ancient chief at college with a royal author grows boring.
explanation.walkthrough: Uther Pendragon is the legendary British king, father of Arthur.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary ruler of the Britons and father of King Arthur, a warlord of the sixth century.

clue.text: Container for Percy's ballads?

parts.note: Thomas Percy collected old songs in Reliques of Ancient English Poetry, so a box of relics would house them

explanation.surface: Asks what holds a collection of old songs.
explanation.walkthrough: Bishop Percy's 1765 anthology was called Reliques, so its container is a shrine for relics.
explanation.definitionFit: A casket or shrine for holy relics, punning on the title of Percy's anthology.

clue.text: Friendly as Kingsley, perhaps?

parts.note: the novelist Kingsley Amis lends his surname, and a word for friendly sounds like his name plus 'able'

explanation.surface: Wonders whether a certain Kingsley was genial.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley Amis, the comic novelist: the word for friendly starts like 'Amis', as if it meant 'Amis-able'.
explanation.definitionFit: Means good-natured and peaceable, here jokingly linked to the surname of Kingsley Amis.

clue.text: Leading lady, colleague of Nicholas, able to do anything but none of it very well

definitions.text: Leading lady, colleague of Nicholas, able to do anything but none of it very well

parts.words: Leading lady, colleague of Nicholas, able to do anything but none of it very well
parts.note: describes the actress of the Crummles company who acts alongside Nicholas in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby

explanation.surface: Portrait of a versatile but mediocre stage star who works with Nicholas.
explanation.walkthrough: In Nicholas Nickleby the hero joins Vincent Crummles's touring theatre, whose leading lady is a flirtatious, multi-talented but middling performer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dickens actress in the Crummles troupe, Nicholas Nickleby's stage partner during his time as a player.

clue.text: Diabolic novel verses

definitions.meaning: Salman Rushdie's novel is The ... Verses

explanation.surface: A devilish novel of poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish, belonging to the Devil; also the first word of the title of Rushdie's novel.

clue.text: Empress found in car Nazi wrecked

indicators.note: the car is smashed up, so the letters of car and Nazi are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Russian empress is discovered in a fascist's crashed vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: The wife of a tsar, or a female Russian ruler.

clue.text: Written while confined, like De Profundis?

definitions.meaning: shut in a pen or enclosure; Wilde wrote De Profundis in Reading Gaol

explanation.surface: Something composed while locked up, like Wilde's prison letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Means both composed in writing and shut in a pen, and Wilde's letter was both.

clue.text: Odette's showy bloomers of unique significance to Swann

definitions.text: Odette's showy bloomers of unique significance to Swann

parts.words: Odette's showy bloomers of unique significance to Swann
parts.note: in Proust, Swann first makes love to Odette while adjusting the orchids at her bodice, and 'doing' these flowers becomes their private phrase

explanation.surface: A lady's flamboyant blooms, or knickers, mean something special to her lover.
explanation.walkthrough: In Proust's Swann's Way, 'faire catleya' becomes Swann and Odette's code for making love, from the orchids she wore.
explanation.definitionFit: A genus of showy tropical orchids, which Odette wears and which become Swann's private euphemism.

clue.text: He took all in Greeneland

parts.note: 'Greeneland' is the critics' name for Greene's fictional world

explanation.surface: Someone scoops the pot in Graham Greene's world.
explanation.walkthrough: The title of Greene's 1955 novella says that the one who fails takes all.
explanation.definitionFit: One who is beaten, the paradoxical winner in Greene's title Loser Takes All.

clue.text: Strange Behan chap, though conventional on Sunday

indicators.note: the abbreviation for Sunday sits on the front of the answer to give the word for conventional, so take it off

parts.note: square means old-fashioned and conventional

explanation.surface: Brendan Behan's odd fellow becomes respectable on the Sabbath.
explanation.walkthrough: Behan's play is The Quare Fellow; 'quare' is Irish dialect for strange. With S for Sunday put on, it becomes conventional SQUARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish dialect form of queer, meaning odd or peculiar, as in Behan's title The Quare Fellow.

clue.text: S-f writer does aerial turn

definitions.meaning: an aircraft tilts its wings to turn

explanation.definitionFit: Iain M. Banks wrote the Culture novels; an aircraft tilts sideways as it turns.

clue.text: Publicity speech by some knowledgeable chaps at the Uffizi

definitions.text: some knowledgeable chaps at the Uffizi

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement
an oration is a formal speech

explanation.surface: Wise men in a Florentine gallery deliver a promotional address.
explanation.walkthrough: The Uffizi in Florence holds several paintings of the Adoration of the Magi, the three wise men.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adoration of the Magi is a painting subject showing the wise men worshipping the infant Christ.

clue.text: Academician comes back with model to produce painting

indicators.note: the academician turns back, so its letters are read in reverse

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician
the Model T was Ford's famous car

explanation.surface: A Royal Academy member returns with a sitter to create a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Painting is a form of visual creative work.

clue.text: Cutting passage

definitions.meaning: a clipping taken from a text
a section of a written work

explanation.definitionFit: An extract is a clipping or a quoted section from a longer work.

clue.text: "I'll be sworn you would believe my saying, / Howe'er you lean to the —" (The Winter's Tale)

definitions.text: "I'll be sworn you would believe my saying, / Howe'er you lean to the —" (The Winter's Tale)

parts.words: "I'll be sworn you would believe my saying, / Howe'er you lean to the —" (The Winter's Tale)
parts.note: the missing word from Leontes's lines in Shakespeare's play means the side of denial

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with a blank to fill.
explanation.definitionFit: Toward refusal or denial, the opposite inclination to agreement.
